'''Eugene Ernest Haller''' (January 5, 1943 – June 22, 2018) was a [[Switzerland|Swiss]]-American [[physicist]] and [[Materials science|materials scientist]].  

== Early life and career ==
Haller studied physics at the [[University of Basel]] and graduated in 1967 with a thesis in [[nuclear physics]]. In 1970, he received his doctorate with a thesis in [[solid-state physics]] and [[applied physics]]. In the same year, he moved to the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] in [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]], initially on a three-year scholarship from the [[Swiss National Science Foundation]] and subsequently as a research assistant. In 1980, he was appointed [[associate professor]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and two years later he was promoted to [[Professor|full professor]]. He remained there until his retirement in 2011, while also working as a senior scientist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Since 2005, he had held the Liao-Cho Innovation Endowed Chair at UC Berkeley.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Hernandez |first=Daisy |date=2018-06-24 |title=Eugene Haller, leading expert in semiconductor materials, dies at 75 |url=https://mse.berkeley.edu/2018/06/eugene-haller-leading-expert-in-semiconductor-materials-dies-at-75/ |access-date=2025-12-20 |website=Materials Science & Engineering, University of California |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Wu |first=Junqiao |last2=Dubón Jr. |first2=Oscar |last3=Van de Walle |first3=Chris G. |title=Professor Eugene Ernest Haller |url=https://nae.edu/30151/Professor-Eugene-Ernest-Haller |access-date=2025-12-20 |website=National Academy of Engineering |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Wu |first=Junqiao |last2=Dubon Jr. |first2=Oscar |date=2018 |title=Eugene E. Haller |url=https://senate.universityofcalifornia.edu/in-memoriam/files/eugene-haller.html |access-date=2025-12-20 |website=University of California}}</ref> 

== Research ==
With his research into the synthesis of high-purity and [[Doping (semiconductor)|doped]] crystals, Haller made contributions to improving the quality of [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]]. His advances in the growth of semiconductor crystals led to the production of [[germanium]] of unprecedented purity. This formed the basis for one of the three scientific instruments (Multiband Imaging Photometer) on the [[Spitzer Space Telescope]], launched in 2003.<ref name=":1" /> Haller also demonstrated the significant influence of [[hydrogen]] on semiconductors and was one of the first to recognize the potential of [[Isotope|isotopes]] in semiconductor manufacturing.

In 1984, he founded the Electronic Materials Program at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, a program funded by the [[United States Department of Energy]] that continues to this day. In 1986, he spent a research stay at the [[Max Planck Institute for Solid State Research]] in [[Stuttgart]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Prof. Dr. Eugene E. Haller |url=https://www.humboldt-foundation.de/vernetzen/recherche-im-humboldt-netzwerk/einzelansicht/1009909/prof-dr-eugene-e-haller |access-date=2025-12-20 |website=Alexander von Humboldt-Stiftung |language=de}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
He was married to his wife Marianne and was the father of two daughters, Isabelle and Nicole.<ref name=":0" /> In his private life, he collected historic radios and owned a 1939 [[Talbot-Lago|Talbot Lago]] T23 classic car.<ref name=":1" /> 

== Awards and honors ==
* 1985: [[Humboldt Research Award]] for Scientists from the U.S.<ref name=":3" />
* 1986: Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS)<ref name=":1" />
* 1990: Miller Research Professorship<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Haller |first=Eugene E. |date=2006-07-01 |title=Isotopically Controlled Semiconductors |url=https://doi.org/10.1557/mrs2006.141 |journal=MRS Bulletin |language=en |volume=31 |issue=7 |pages=547–553 |doi=10.1557/mrs2006.141 |issn=1938-1425|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* 1994: Max Planck Research Award<ref name=":4" />
* 1999: [[James C. McGroddy Prize]] for New Materials from the American Physical Society<ref name=":2" />
* 2001: Miller Research Professorship<ref name=":4" />
* 2004: Member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS)<ref name=":1" />
* 2005: David Turnbull Lectureship from the [[Materials Research Society]]<ref name=":2" />
* 2010: FMD John Bardeen Award of [[The Minerals, Metals & Materials Society]]<ref name=":2" />
* 2010: Member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]]<ref name=":1" />
